title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F23
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 42 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for a narrative about Amazon deforestation. Read the complete narrative to identify the study area and environmental issue discussed. Download the relevant satellite assets: select a Sentinel-2 false-colour image covering the same region during the dry season (July–September 2022). Summarize the visible evidence of deforestation or forest degradation and explain how it supports or challenges the findings described in the narrative.

answers.text:
Based on the narrative "Forests on the Brink: Satellite Imagery unveiling Loss and Shifting Forest Landscapes" and the Sentinel-2 false-color composite image of the Amazon region, here is the analysis:

Study Area and Environmental Issue
The narrative discusses global forest loss and degradation, with a specific focus on the Amazon rainforest as a critical region. The environmental issues include:
• Biodiversity Loss: Forests host 75% of terrestrial biodiversity.
• Carbon Emissions: Deforestation contributes to 15% of global carbon emissions.
• Climate Regulation: Forests regulate local and global climates by maintaining energy balance and water cycles.
• Human Impact: Deforestation disrupts ecosystem services vital for human livelihoods.

Visible Evidence from the Image
The false-color composite image, which uses bands B8 (NIR), B4 (Red), and B3 (Green), is designed to highlight vegetation health. In this composite:
• Healthy Vegetation: Appears in bright red or pink (high NIR reflectance).
• Degraded or Deforested Areas: Appear in dark tones or black (low NIR reflectance).

In the provided image, we observe:
• Large areas of dark tones/black (likely deforested or degraded land).
• Contrasting bright red/pink areas (likely healthy vegetation).

Support or Challenge to Narrative Findings
The image strongly supports the narrative's findings:
1. Deforestation Evidence: The dark areas in the image correspond to deforested or degraded land, which aligns with the narrative's claim that deforestation is occurring at alarming rates in the Amazon.
2. Biodiversity and Carbon Impact: The visible deforestation in the image underscores the narrative's point that deforestation threatens biodiversity and contributes significantly to carbon emissions.
3. Climate Regulation: The image visually demonstrates the extent of land-use change, which can disrupt local and global climate patterns as mentioned in the narrative.

Conclusion
The Sentinel-2 false-color composite image provides clear visual evidence of deforestation and forest degradation in the Amazon region, supporting the narrative's claims about the severity and urgency of the issue. The image highlights the need for continued monitoring and action to address deforestation and its environmental impacts.

Based on the Sentinel-2 false-color image of Manaus, Brazil, acquired in August 2022 (a dry season month), here is an analysis of the visible evidence of deforestation or forest degradation and how it relates to the findings in the EO Dashboard narrative:

Visible Evidence in the Image

The image uses a false-color composite (B06, B08, B04) where:
• Healthy vegetation appears red (B08, NIR band).
• Water bodies appear dark blue/black.
• Urban areas and cleared land appear lighter shades (often white or gray).

In the image, the vast majority of the area is covered in dense, healthy green vegetation (red in false color), indicating a largely intact rainforest. However, there are several notable features:

1.  Urban Area (Manaus): The city of Manaus is visible as a cluster of bright white/gray pixels in the lower right quadrant. This represents the urban footprint, which is a clear sign of land conversion from natural forest to human infrastructure. This is a form of forest degradation, as the natural ecosystem is replaced by built environments.

2.  Linear Clearings and Roads: Darker, linear features cutting through the green canopy, particularly visible in the upper left and center, likely represent roads, rivers, or other linear infrastructure. These are often precursors to deforestation, as they provide access for logging, agriculture, or other land uses.

3.  Patchy Clearings: There are some smaller, irregularly shaped patches of lighter color scattered throughout the forest, which could indicate small-scale deforestation or agricultural activities.

Comparison with the Narrative

The narrative "A view from space monitors land cover and tree to track aboveground biomass and carbon content" discusses the broader context of deforestation and forest degradation in the Amazon basin, emphasizing its global impact on carbon emissions and climate change.

• Supporting Evidence: The image provides direct visual confirmation of the narrative's point that human activity (urbanization, infrastructure development) leads to forest degradation. The clear distinction between the urban area and the surrounding forest visually demonstrates the land-use change that the narrative describes as a key driver of carbon emissions.

• Limitations of the Image: While the image shows clear evidence of degradation, it does not provide the detailed, large-scale deforestation patterns or biomass loss metrics that the narrative discusses. The narrative focuses on the global impact and the use of satellite data for monitoring, while this single image provides a localized snapshot of degradation. The image does not show the extent of deforestation or the specific biomass loss mentioned in the narrative, which would require more detailed analysis of the STAC collections (like RECCAP2_6_deforested_biomass) mentioned in the narrative.

In conclusion, the Sentinel-2 image supports the narrative's claim that human activity leads to forest degradation in the Amazon. It provides a clear visual example of this process, specifically urban expansion and infrastructure development, which are significant contributors to the environmental issue discussed. However, the image is a localized view and does not capture the full scale of deforestation or the specific biomass metrics mentioned in the narrative.

Visible Evidence of Deforestation or Forest Degradation

The image, rendered in false color (B08, B04, B03), shows the Amazon rainforest with a dominant red hue, indicating dense vegetation. However, the presence of dark, winding lines (likely rivers) and scattered darker patches suggests areas of potential forest degradation or deforestation. These darker patches may represent:

1. Deforested Areas: Clearings or agricultural land where vegetation has been removed, appearing as dark spots against the red background.
2. Forest Degradation: Areas with reduced vegetation density or canopy cover, possibly due to selective logging or other disturbances, which appear as darker patches or mottled textures.
3. Water Bodies: The dark winding lines are likely rivers or streams, which appear dark in false-color imagery due to their water content and lack of vegetation.

Support or Challenge to Narrative Findings

The narrative highlights the global issue of deforestation and forest degradation, emphasizing biodiversity loss, climate impacts, and the role of satellite monitoring. The image supports these findings in the following ways:

1. Visual Confirmation of Forest Cover: The dominant red color indicates extensive forest cover, aligning with the narrative’s emphasis on the Amazon as a critical biodiversity hotspot.
2. Evidence of Degradation: The darker patches and lines suggest localized disturbances, supporting the narrative’s claim that deforestation and degradation are occurring at alarming rates, even if not explicitly quantified in the image.
3. Role of Satellite Monitoring: The image exemplifies how satellite imagery (like Sentinel-2) can visually identify and monitor forest changes, reinforcing the narrative’s assertion that such technology is crucial for tracking and addressing forest loss.

Conclusion

The Sentinel-2 image provides visual evidence of both intact forest cover and potential areas of degradation or deforestation in the Amazon region. This supports the narrative’s broader message about the global challenge of forest loss and the importance of satellite monitoring in addressing it. The image underscores the need for continued efforts to protect and restore forests, as highlighted in the Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use.

Top Paper: Next Day Wildfire Spread: A Machine Learning Data Set to Predict Wildfire Spreading from Remote-Sensing Data
Authors: Fantine Huot, R. Lily Hu, Nita Goyal, Tharun Sankar, Matthias Ihme, Yi-Fan Chen
Published: December 4, 2021
Categories: Computer Vision (cs.CV)
URL: arXiv:2112.02447v2 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.02447v2.pdf)

Abstract:
Predicting wildfire spread is critical for land management and disaster preparedness. To this end, we present Next Day Wildfire Spread, a curated, large-scale, multivariate dataset of historical wildfires aggregating nearly a decade of remote-sensing data across the United States. In contrast to existing fire datasets based on Earth observation satellites, our dataset combines 2D fire data with multiple explanatory variables (e.g., topography, vegetation, weather, drought index, population density) aligned over 2D regions, providing a feature-rich dataset for machine learning. To demonstrate the usefulness of this dataset, we implement a neural network that takes advantage of the spatial information of this data to predict wildfire spread. We compare the performance of the neural network with other machine learning models: logistic regression and random forest. This dataset can be used as a benchmark for developing wildfire propagation models based on remote sensing data for a lead time of one day.

Abstract:
The paper proposes using Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of a thermal turbulent boundary layer (TTBL) as an analogy to simulate bushfires. This approach serves as a testbed for AI-enhanced remote sensing of bushfire propagation. By solving the Navier-Stokes equations, DNS predicts the flow field and interactions between turbulent flow and thermal plumes, generating synthetic remote sensing data to train AI algorithms like CNNs and RNNs. This method aims to improve the accuracy of AI remote sensing in predicting firefront propagation and assessing the performance of prediction models. The combination of DNS and AI is expected to enhance bushfire management and mitigation strategies.
